questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to boost your immune system
Where Covid-19 came from and how serious it may be
How vaccines against SARS were developed
Why bats are dangerous to humans
questions.why: Neil says they'll look at the origins of Covid-19 and new evidence about the scale of the threat.

questions.q: What do we learn about the SARS outbreak of 2002–2004?
options: It only affected people in Europe and North America
It spread widely but caused no deaths at all
It was caused by bacteria, not by a virus
It killed hundreds in southern China and then spread
questions.why: Georgina says it caused hundreds of deaths in southern China before spreading elsewhere.

questions.q: How did the SARS virus survive and create new strains?
options: By changing as it reproduced in infected people
By hiding for a long time in water supplies
By staying frozen in ice for many years
By infecting only wild animals, never humans
questions.why: Neil says it survived by mutating as it reproduced in infected people, creating strains.

questions.q: How many types of coronavirus carried by bats did a Chinese research project find?
options: About 70
About 7
Over 700
Over 7,000
questions.why: Georgina says a project in China identified over 700 types of coronavirus carried by bats.

questions.q: What does Dr Peter Daszak say would have been even better than finding the precursor to SARS 2?
options: Finding a cure for SARS 1 at the same time
Finding it early enough to warn people and stop it
Proving that bats were not involved in any way
Finding a completely new type of bat in the caves
questions.why: He says it would have been better to find it before SARS 2 emerged and raise the red flag.

questions.q: What was Dr Daszak's team looking for in bats?
options: A cure for coronavirus hidden in their blood
A completely new disease that nobody knew about
Bats that were naturally immune to all viruses
The original SARS virus, thought to have gone
questions.why: He says their hypothesis was that SARS 1, thought to have disappeared, was still out there in bats.

questions.q: What did Professor Mary Fowkes notice about Covid-19?
options: It only attacks the lungs and nothing else
It is much less dangerous than SARS 1 was
It also damages the brain, blood and other organs
It affects only older patients with health problems
questions.why: Georgina says she noticed Covid-19 was damaging the brain, blood and other organs too.

questions.q: Why does Professor Fowkes mention the loss of sense of smell?
options: As a sign that the virus affects the brain
As proof the patient will recover quickly
As a sign of a lung infection
As a side effect of medicine
questions.why: She says loss of smell 'is a direct connection to the brain as well'.
